items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "fictive kin".
items.answer: People treated as kin, such as godparents or close family friends, although not related by descent or marriage
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: people treated as kin, such as godparents or close family friends, although not related by descent or marriage. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why anthropologists describe kinship as cultural rather than simply biological.
items.answer: Societies differ in who counts as kin, how relatives are classified, and how kinship is created (by birth, marriage, adoption, feeding or choice); biological ties are interpreted and sometimes overridden by cultural rules.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Societies differ in who counts as kin, how relatives are classified, and how kinship is created (by birth, marriage, adoption, feeding or choice); biological ties are interpreted and sometimes overridden by cultural rules. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Priya writes: "Kinship is the same as biological relatedness everywhere." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Kinship is culturally defined; Carsten showed kinship created by sharing food and Weston showed chosen families based on care.
items.markingKey: Kinship is culturally defined; Carsten showed kinship created by sharing food and Weston showed chosen families based on care. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Carsten's study of kinship on Langkawi, Malaysia as an example, explain kinship as a cultural process.
items.answer: Carsten found that people become kin by living in the same house and eating rice cooked on the same hearth. Kinship is made through everyday practices of feeding and co-residence, not only given at birth.
items.markingKey: Context (Carsten found that people become kin by living in the same house and eating rice cooked on the same hearth.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: kinship is made through everyday practices of feeding and co-residence, not only given at birth. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to kinship as a cultural process.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

When Grandmother Adwoa died, the family meeting was held in her abusua's house, not in her husband's. Her son Kofi, a lawyer in Accra, expected to inherit her cocoa farm, but the elders announced that it would go to her sister's son, Yaw. Kofi argued that his father had cleared the land. "Your father's line is your father's," the eldest woman said. "Your mother's land goes to her blood." That evening, Kofi drew me a family tree on a napkin, with arrows pointing to everyone who would "eat" from the farm.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a family meeting in the Ashanti region of Ghana.

Using the key concept of social relations, explain how kinship rules shape inheritance in the text. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: Akan matrilineal descent places a woman's property in her abusua, so inheritance passes to her sister's son rather than her own son, who belongs to her lineage but whose claim is weakened by his father's contribution; this reveals tension between matrilineal rules and conjugal or paternal claims, and Kofi's napkin diagram shows kinship as a map of rights to resources.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Akan matrilineal descent places a woman's property in her abusua, so inheritance passes to her sister's son rather than her own son, who belongs to her lineage but whose claim is weakened by his father's contribution; this reveals tension between matrilineal rules and conjugal or paternal claims, and Kofi's napkin diagram shows kinship as a map of rights to resources. items.stem: Using Lévi-Strauss's structuralism (in comparative analyses of kinship and of Amerindian myths from South America) as your example, describe how culture is shown.
items.answer: Lévi-Strauss argued that the human mind orders the world through binary oppositions such as raw/cooked and nature/culture, and that myths work through these oppositions.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Lévi-Strauss argued that the human mind orders the world through binary oppositions such as raw/cooked and nature/culture, and that myths work through these oppositions. Award up to [5]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Claude Lévi-Strauss, The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949) and The Raw and the Cooked (1964), in comparative analyses of kinship and of Amerindian myths from South America); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to culture. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Kinship remains the central organising principle of social life."
items.answer: Kinship is still central in many domains, though its importance varies with the role of state and market.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it shapes inheritance, marriage and care everywhere; migrant networks rely on kin. Arguments against: states, markets and institutions organise much of life in industrial societies; friendship and chosen families compete with kinship. Supported judgement: Kinship is still central in many domains, though its importance varies with the role of state and market.

items.stem: Briefly explain why kinship terminologies reveal how a society classifies relatives.
items.answer: Grouping relatives under one term (father and father's brother) suggests similar rights and duties, so terminologies show which distinctions matter socially.

items.stem: Distinguish between consanguinity and affinity.
items.answer: Consanguinity is relationship by descent; affinity is relationship by marriage. Societies differ in how they weigh each.
items.markingKey: Consanguinity is relationship by descent; affinity is relationship by marriage. Societies differ in how they weigh each. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Descent traced through males only, so children belong to their father's group"?
items.answer: patrilineal descent
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of patrilineal descent.

items.stem: Briefly explain why descent groups can change in importance.
items.answer: Wage labour, state law, migration and urbanisation weaken the economic and political functions of lineages, as with the decline of the Nayar taravad, though lineages may retain ritual or identity roles.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Wage labour, state law, migration and urbanisation weaken the economic and political functions of lineages, as with the decline of the Nayar taravad, though lineages may retain ritual or identity roles. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a clan and a lineage.
items.answer: A lineage is a descent group whose members can demonstrate their genealogical links to a known ancestor; a clan is larger and its members stipulate descent from a common, often mythical, ancestor.
items.markingKey: A lineage is a descent group whose members can demonstrate their genealogical links to a known ancestor; a clan is larger and its members stipulate descent from a common, often mythical, ancestor. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the clan gathering in a rented hall in Nairobi, three hundred people wearing the same printed cloth sit by lineage. The elder who opens the meeting recites the names of nine generations back to the founding ancestor. A young accountant, Wanjiku, keeps a spreadsheet of members' contributions to the clan school-fees fund. When a man from Mombasa claims membership, two elders question him about his grandfather's village. He passes when he names the right river. "In the city," Wanjiku tells me, "the clan is our insurance company."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a clan meeting in Nairobi, Kenya.

Using the key concept of belonging, explain how the text shows a descent group adapting to urban life. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: The clan still uses descent (genealogical recitation, lineage seating, testing a claim through ancestral place) to define belonging, but it now functions in the city as a mutual-aid and financial institution (school fees, "insurance company"), using modern tools (spreadsheet), showing descent groups changing function rather than disappearing.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Matrilineal societies give women more power than patrilineal ones."
items.answer: Matriliny often gives women property and status, but it does not automatically produce female political power.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: women control houses and land among the Minangkabau (Sanday); Trobriand women hold public power in exchange (Weiner). Arguments against: mother's brothers often hold authority (matrilineal puzzle); power depends also on economy, religion and the state. Supported judgement: Matriliny often gives women property and status, but it does not automatically produce female political power.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "descent".
items.answer: The principle by which a person is recognised as a member of a kin group through a parent or line of ancestors
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the principle by which a person is recognised as a member of a kin group through a parent or line of ancestors. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Nia writes: "Matrilineal societies are ruled by women." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Matriliny concerns descent and inheritance; authority is often held by men as mother's brothers, although women may have significant property and influence.
items.markingKey: Matriliny concerns descent and inheritance; authority is often held by men as mother's brothers, although women may have significant property and influence. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "endogamy"?
options: The system of terms a society uses for relatives, which shows how relatives are classified, e.g. whether father and father's brother share one term
The rule requiring people to marry within a defined group such as their caste, religion or community
A descent group whose members can trace their actual genealogical links to a known common ancestor
Relationship through shared descent ("blood"), such as between parent and child or between siblings
items.answer: The rule requiring people to marry within a defined group such as their caste, religion or community
items.markingKey: B. "endogamy" is the rule requiring people to marry within a defined group such as their caste, religion or community.

items.stem: Distinguish between dowry and bridewealth.
items.answer: Bridewealth is paid by the groom's kin to the bride's kin and transfers rights over the bride's children and labour; dowry is property given with the bride, from her own family, at marriage.
items.markingKey: Bridewealth is paid by the groom's kin to the bride's kin and transfers rights over the bride's children and labour; dowry is property given with the bride, from her own family, at marriage. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why rules of exogamy create alliances.
items.answer: Requiring marriage outside one's group forces groups to exchange spouses, creating lasting ties and obligations between them (Lévi-Strauss). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Requiring marriage outside one's group forces groups to exchange spouses, creating lasting ties and obligations between them (Lévi-Strauss). items.stem:
Read the text below.

The negotiations for Thandiwe's lobola took place in her uncle's sitting room in Soweto. Her father did not speak; her uncles did. The groom's delegation began by paying a small "door-opening" fee before they were allowed to sit. The amount was discussed in cattle, though everyone knew it would be paid by bank transfer. Thandiwe, a pharmacist, laughed afterwards: "They valued me at eleven cows. My degree counted for two." Her mother added: "It is not a price. It is so they know we love her."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a lobola (bridewealth) negotiation in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Describe how the lobola negotiation was conducted, as presented in the text. Use brief quotations from the text to support each point you make.
items.answer: It took place in her uncle's sitting room; her uncles negotiated and her father stayed silent; the groom's delegation paid a "door-opening" fee before sitting; the amount was discussed in cattle but paid by bank transfer; her education raised the amount (two of eleven cows).
items.markingKey: It took place in her uncle's sitting room; her uncles negotiated and her father stayed silent; the groom's delegation paid a "door-opening" fee before sitting; the amount was discussed in cattle but paid by bank transfer; her education raised the amount (two of eleven cows). items.stem: Briefly describe Yan's study of Xiajia village, China and explain what it reveals about change in marriage exchange.
items.answer: From the 1980s bridewealth rose sharply and was increasingly controlled by the bride and groom, who used it to set up their own household. Marriage payments were reinterpreted as an early inheritance for the new couple, showing the rise of conjugal independence.
items.markingKey: Context (From the 1980s bridewealth rose sharply and was increasingly controlled by the bride and groom, who used it to set up their own household.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: marriage payments were reinterpreted as an early inheritance for the new couple, showing the rise of conjugal independence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to change in marriage exchange.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Marriage is primarily an alliance between groups rather than a relationship between individuals."
items.answer: Marriage combines alliance and personal relationship; the balance shifts with economic and social change.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: bridewealth and exogamy link lineages (Nuer, Lévi-Strauss); families negotiate marriages and payments. Arguments against: romantic love and individual choice have grown (Yan); same-sex and companionate marriage emphasise individuals; both dimensions coexist. Supported judgement: Marriage combines alliance and personal relationship; the balance shifts with economic and social change.

items.stem: Explain why residence patterns matter for women's lives.
items.answer: Where a couple lives determines whose kin surround the wife, her access to support and property, and her power in the household; patrilocal residence may isolate a bride among her husband's relatives.

items.stem: Distinguish between genetic parenthood and social parenthood.
items.answer: Genetic parenthood is the provision of the egg or sperm; social parenthood is raising and being recognised as the parent. ART can separate the two.

items.stem: "Reproductive technologies have made kinship purely a matter of genetics." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: ART forces choices about which tie counts – genetic, gestational or intentional – and societies answer differently (Kahn, Inhorn), showing kinship remains cultural.
items.markingKey: ART forces choices about which tie counts – genetic, gestational or intentional – and societies answer differently (Kahn, Inhorn), showing kinship remains cultural. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline how social relations shapes new kinship, chosen kin and reproductive technologies, using evidence from Kahn's Reproducing Jews.
items.answer: Because Jewishness passes through the mother in rabbinic law, debates arose over whether a child born from a donor egg takes the identity of the egg donor or of the woman who gives birth.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that new kinship studies have replaced older approaches to kinship. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: New kinship studies have transformed the field but complement rather than replace descent and alliance analysis.

items.stem: Lévi-Strauss's alliance theory argues that marriage is fundamentally:
options: an exchange that creates links between groups
a contract between two individuals only

items.answer: The term avoids assuming that kinship is defined by biology, allowing anthropologists to study how people create connection through food, houses, care and other practices in their own terms.

items.answer: A classificatory terminology groups some lineal and collateral relatives under the same term; a descriptive terminology uses separate terms that describe the exact relationship.

items.stem: Explain why matrilineal descent does not mean that women hold political power.
items.answer: In many matrilineal societies, authority over the lineage is held by men, especially the mother's brother; descent and power are separate dimensions, though matriliny can give women property and influence (Minangkabau).

items.answer: Marriage varies widely – polygyny, polyandry, same-sex marriage, the Nayar case – so anthropologists use broad definitions focused on rights and legitimacy.

items.stem: Distinguish between social parenthood and genetic parenthood.
items.answer: Genetic parenthood is the provision of the egg or sperm; social parenthood is raising and being recognised as the parent. ART can separate the two.

items.stem: Distinguish between affinity and consanguinity.
items.answer: Consanguinity is relationship by descent; affinity is relationship by marriage. Societies differ in how they weigh each.
items.markingKey: Consanguinity is relationship by descent; affinity is relationship by marriage. Societies differ in how they weigh each. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Identify one way in which social relations matters in Gough's study of the Nayar (on the Nayar of Kerala, south India, as they lived before twentieth-century legal reforms) and explain its significance.
items.answer: Nayar girls underwent a tali-tying rite before puberty; later they could take several visiting sambandham partners, while children belonged to their mother's matrilineal household (taravad).

items.stem: With reference to Claude Lévi-Strauss, The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949) and The Raw and the Cooked (1964), explain how the key concept of social relations helps us to understand marriage, exchange and residence.
items.answer: In alliance theory, the incest taboo forces groups to exchange women in marriage, creating bonds between groups; the taboo marks the passage from nature to culture.

At the Sunday lunch, there are fourteen people around two tables pushed together: Leo and Marcus, their twin daughters born through a surrogate in Canada, Marcus's ex-wife, her new partner, two of Leo's colleagues the girls call "uncle", and Marcus's mother, who cooks. The surrogate, Jenna, joins on a video call from Ontario. When one twin asks why Jenna is not "a mummy", Marcus's mother answers: "She helped you come. I feed you. Daddy and Papa are your parents." Everyone laughs; Jenna waves.

Analyse how the text shows kinship as relatedness created through practice. Support your answer with evidence from the text. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.

The negotiations for Thandiwe's lobola took place in her uncle's sitting room in Soweto. Her father did not speak; her uncles did. Thandiwe, a pharmacist, laughed afterwards: "They valued me at eleven cows. My degree counted for two." Her mother added: "It is not a price. It is so they know we love her."

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "cognatic (bilateral) descent"?

items.stem: With reference to Nuer bridewealth (Evans-Pritchard), explain how it illustrates marriage as transfer of rights.

At the clan gathering in a rented hall in Nairobi, three hundred people wearing the same printed cloth sit by lineage. The elder who opens the meeting recites the names of nine generations back to the founding ancestor. "In the city," Wanjiku tells me, "the clan is our insurance company."

Read the text below.

At the Sunday lunch, there are fourteen people around two tables pushed together: Leo and Marcus, their twin daughters born through a surrogate in Canada, Marcus's ex-wife, her new partner, two of Leo's colleagues the girls call "uncle", and Marcus's mother, who cooks. The surrogate, Jenna, joins on a video call from Ontario. When one twin asks why Jenna is not "a mummy", Marcus's mother answers: "She helped you come. I feed you. Daddy and Papa are your parents." Everyone laughs; Jenna waves.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a family lunch in Amsterdam.

Compare the significance of social relations in the text with its significance in Strathern's The Gender of the Gift. Refer explicitly to the ethnographic context of both. Your answer should identify both similarities and differences.
items.answer: Text: Kinship here combines law (Daddy and Papa as parents), choice (colleagues as "uncles"), ex-partners and technology (surrogacy, video call); the grandmother distinguishes roles by practice – helping them "come", feeding, parenting – echoing Carsten's relatedness through feeding and Weston's chosen families; the surrogate's role is acknowledged but classified differently from motherhood. Ethnography – Marilyn Strathern, The Gender of the Gift (1988), drawing on her fieldwork in Mount Hagen, Papua New Guinea, and Melanesian ethnography: Exchange of pigs and shells in ceremonial moka creates and displays relationships, so persons are made through what they give and receive. Comparison: similarities and differences in how social relations is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.
